summary: Magnesium bisglycinate is a chelated form of magnesium in which the mineral is bound to two molecules of the amino acid glycine. It is used as an oral dietary supplement to prevent or correct magnesium deficiency and to support normal nerve, muscle and metabolic function; the chelated form is generally better tolerated (less laxative effect) and reasonably well absorbed compared with inorganic salts such as magnesium oxide. Typical adult supplementation provides about 200-400 mg of elemental magnesium per day in divided doses, ideally taken with food and kept within the tolerable upper intake level for supplemental magnesium (350 mg/day of elemental magnesium for adults from supplements, per the US Institute of Medicine). It is NOT an FDA-approved drug - it is regulated as a dietary supplement - so guidance follows dietary-reference-intake and supplement references rather than an FDA drug label. The main risks are diarrhoea/GI upset and, importantly, hypermagnesaemia in people with significant renal impairment.
indications: Prevention and treatment of dietary magnesium deficiency / inadequate intake
Nutritional support where magnesium needs are increased (e.g. with certain medications or chronic alcohol use)
General supplementation to support normal muscle and nerve function (supplement claim)

admin: Take orally with food to improve absorption and minimise gastrointestinal/laxative effects
Divide larger daily amounts into 2 or more doses to reduce the risk of diarrhoea
Check the label for the elemental magnesium content - dose by elemental magnesium, not total salt weight
Separate from certain medicines that magnesium can chelate (e.g. some antibiotics, bisphosphonates, levothyroxine) by a few hours
Avoid exceeding the tolerable upper intake level for supplemental magnesium unless directed by a clinician
Use cautiously and under supervision in anyone with significant kidney disease
moa: Magnesium is an essential cofactor for over 300 enzymatic reactions, including ATP-dependent processes, oxidative phosphorylation, protein and nucleic-acid synthesis, and the regulation of nerve conduction, neuromuscular transmission and muscle contraction. As a calcium and NMDA-receptor modulator it stabilises excitable membranes. In the bisglycinate chelate the magnesium is bound to glycine, which is thought to favour intact absorption across the intestinal wall (partly via amino-acid pathways) and to reduce the osmotic/laxative effect seen with poorly absorbed inorganic salts. Once absorbed, the magnesium replenishes body stores and supports these physiological functions.

absolute: Severe renal impairment / renal failure (risk of hypermagnesaemia)
relative: Moderate renal impairment (use lower doses with monitoring)
Myasthenia gravis (magnesium can worsen neuromuscular weakness)
monitor: Serum magnesium, especially in renal impairment
Signs of hypermagnesaemia (weakness, low blood pressure, slowed reflexes)

preg: Magnesium at recommended dietary/supplemental intakes is generally considered safe in pregnancy and adequate intake is important; do not exceed the tolerable upper intake level for supplements without medical advice. (High-dose IV magnesium for obstetric indications is a separate, supervised use.)
lact: Magnesium supplementation at recommended intakes is considered compatible with breastfeeding; magnesium is a normal milk constituent and excess maternal intake has little effect on milk levels in women with normal renal function.
renal: Use with caution and reduce the dose in moderate renal impairment, and generally avoid in severe renal impairment or renal failure, because impaired magnesium excretion can lead to dangerous hypermagnesaemia. Monitor serum magnesium when supplementing such patients.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

major: In severe renal impairment, combination with other magnesium-containing products can cause life-threatening hypermagnesaemia
moderate: Tetracycline and fluoroquinolone antibiotics - magnesium chelates them and reduces their absorption; separate dosing by several hours
Bisphosphonates and levothyroxine - reduced absorption; separate dosing
Digoxin, some iron salts - reduced absorption when taken together
minor: Potassium-sparing diuretics - may slightly raise magnesium retention
Proton-pump inhibitors (long-term) can lower magnesium, increasing supplementation need
interactions.food: Take with food to improve tolerance and absorption
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use depletes magnesium and may increase requirements
interactions.diagnostics: Excess intake can raise serum magnesium; monitor magnesium levels where relevant

common: Diarrhoea or loose stools (less than with inorganic salts)
serious: Hypermagnesaemia in renal impairment (muscle weakness, hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory depression)
rare: Cardiac conduction disturbance with severe hypermagnesaemia
emergency: Severe hypermagnesaemia with hypotension, respiratory depression, bradyarrhythmia or cardiac arrest (mainly with renal failure/overdose)

Renal function before and during supplementation in at-risk patients

counsel: Take with food to help absorption and reduce the chance of loose stools
If you get diarrhoea, split the dose through the day or reduce it
Space it a few hours apart from certain antibiotics, thyroid tablets or bisphosphonates, which it can bind to
Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems - magnesium can build up to harmful levels
Do not take more than the recommended amount without advice
This is a supplement, not a prescription medicine - mention it to your pharmacist or doctor
pk: Absorbed over hours; replenishing body stores takes days to weeks of regular intake
Serum magnesium rises modestly within a few hours of a dose
Not a fixed pharmacologic half-life; excess is excreted renally and stores turn over slowly
Daily intake maintains stores; benefit depends on consistent supplementation
Store at room temperature in a dry place, protected from moisture, in the original container
pearls: NOT an FDA-approved drug - regulated as a dietary supplement; guidance follows dietary-reference intakes (supplemental UL ~350 mg elemental magnesium/day for adults)
Chelated (amino-acid-bound) form is better tolerated, with less laxative effect than magnesium oxide/sulfate
Dose by ELEMENTAL magnesium content, not the total salt weight
Hypermagnesaemia is the key danger in renal impairment - use cautiously and monitor
Separate from tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, bisphosphonates and levothyroxine to avoid binding and reduced absorption
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose; in that case skip the missed dose and continue as usual. Do not take a double dose - excess magnesium mainly causes diarrhoea.
overdose: Oral overdose usually causes diarrhoea and abdominal cramps and is self-limiting in people with normal kidney function. In renal impairment or with very large doses, dangerous hypermagnesaemia can occur, causing muscle weakness, low blood pressure, slowed reflexes, bradycardia and respiratory depression. Management is supportive: stop the supplement, give IV fluids, IV calcium gluconate to antagonise cardiac/neuromuscular effects, and dialysis for severe hypermagnesaemia with renal failure.
